tldr: The authors propose Zero-WAM, a causal world-action model that enables a robot to autonomously execute unseen tasks simply by providing a human demonstration video as a prompt. By building an automated pipeline that synthesizes human manipulation videos from robot trajectories, they created a large-scale paired dataset and demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization in both simulation and the real world.
hero_caption: An overview of the automated pipeline for generating large-scale task-paired data and the dataset composition. By sampling existing robot trajectories at the task level and combining VLMs with image and video generation AI, semantically matched human manipulation videos are synthesized to build HumanGen, a large-scale in-context learning dataset of over 74K pairs.
overview:
One of the greatest challenges in robot learning is zero-shot generalization: how to adapt to unseen tasks never encountered during training. In large language models (LLMs), in-context learning (ICL) allows flexible task switching simply by placing instructions in the prompt. For robots, however, language alone often fails to convey spatial constraints and intermediate state transitions.

To address this, the authors came up with the idea of providing the prompt not as language, but as a video of a human performing the task. A video directly conveys the intended visual state changes. However, this approach faced two major hurdles: an extreme scarcity of task-rich paired human-robot data, and shortcut learning where the policy predicts the next action solely from past robot history while ignoring the video prompt. To overcome these issues, they developed an automated pipeline that generates matching human videos from robot trajectories to build HumanGen, a 74.2K-pair dataset, and proposed Zero-WAM, a world-action model with an auxiliary In-context Future chunk Prediction (IFP) objective that forces the model to attend to the video prompt.

They validated the approach on seven unseen tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator and in a real-world environment using a bimanual Franka setup.

As a result, Zero-WAM achieved an average success rate of 46.95% on the unseen simulation tasks, outperforming the strong baseline LingBot-VA (17.45%) by 29.5 percentage points. On the real robot, it demonstrated that unseen task configurations—such as multi-object sequential manipulation and fine-grained assembly—can be solved purely from human video guidance.
contributions: Proposed Zero-WAM, a causal world-action model that takes a human demonstration video or language as a prompt to directly generate actions for unseen tasks.
Constructed HumanGen, an in-context learning dataset consisting of 74.2K pairs across 8.6K tasks, by automatically synthesizing semantically matched human videos from robot trajectories.
Introduced an auxiliary objective, IFP, that suppresses shortcuts learned from seen task histories and forces the policy to capture the long-term intent of the video prompt.

Outperformed the baseline by 29.5 percentage points across seven unseen simulation tasks and demonstrated zero-shot generalization to unseen object arrangements and fine insertion tasks on a real robot.

sections.heading: Bringing Prompt-Based In-Context Learning to Robots with Demonstration Videos
sections.summary: Language instructions alone cannot fully convey spatial and temporal state changes for a robot to execute unseen tasks. This study proposes an in-context learning framework where human demonstration videos are directly provided as context prompts to generate robot actions.
sections.details:
In conventional robot learning, adapting to an unseen task typically requires additional fine-tuning. In the LLM domain, however, in-context learning (ICL)—where a few instructions or demonstrations are given in the prompt—has made solving novel tasks without parameter updates routine. Bringing this paradigm to robotic manipulation is the core motivation of this work.

While recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and video-action models rely predominantly on language instructions, language can only ambiguously capture fine-grained spatial constraints and intermediate object motions. In contrast, showing a video of a human completing the task makes the intended visual evolution of the environment immediately clear.

However, scaling the use of human videos as robot instructions faced two major bottlenecks:

- Paired Data Scarcity: Manually collecting large-scale pairs of human demonstration videos and corresponding executable robot trajectories is prohibitively expensive.
- Shortcut Learning: During training, models can predict the next action solely from recent robot history and text instructions. They learn this shortcut, ignoring the human video, and subsequently fail to attend to novel task videos at test time.

Zero-WAM overcomes both hurdles through a generative AI-based data synthesis pipeline and a new training objective that enforces attention to the long-term flow of the video prompt.

sections.heading: Synthesizing Human Videos from Robot Motions: The 74K-Pair HumanGen Dataset
sections.summary: To solve the scarcity of paired human-robot data, the authors developed a pipeline to automatically synthesize matching human demonstration videos from robot trajectories. Combined with task-balanced sampling, this produced the highly diverse HumanGen dataset.
sections.details:
This section details how the dataset underpinning Zero-WAM was constructed. The key components are task-level sampling and automated human video synthesis using generative AI.

2.1 Task-Diverse Video-Action Data
Existing public robot datasets (such as AgiBot and Open-X-Embodiment) contain vast numbers of trajectories, but many are redundant teleoperation demonstrations of the same tasks. The authors redefined tasks by operation-object combinations and resampled trajectories with a per-task cap. This yielded Task-diverse VA, a pre-training corpus containing about 400K diverse robot trajectories per epoch across over 6,000 tasks.

2.2 In-Context Human Video Generation Pipeline
To scale paired human-robot data, they built a pipeline that synthesizes human manipulation videos from robot trajectories through the following steps:

- A VLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro or Qwen3.6-Plus) analyzes the robot video, extracting the task name as well as initial, intermediate, and final object states.
- An image editing model (Nano Banana 2 or Qwen-Image-2.0) transforms the first frame of the robot video into a human pre-manipulation viewpoint, deliberately varying background, perspective, and object appearance.
- A video generation model (Wan 2.7 or Kling AI 3.0) is prompted to generate a video of a human hand and wrist manipulating the object.
- Finally, a VLM evaluates semantic consistency and physical plausibility, retaining only videos that pass verification.

2.3 In-Context HumanGen Dataset
This process culminated in the HumanGen dataset. It comprises an external pre-training set from public data (5,062 tasks, 41,188 pairs), an internal pre-training set (3,522 tasks, 30,247 pairs), plus simulation and real-world evaluation sets, totaling 8.6K tasks and 74.2K pairs. Compared to existing paired datasets, automated synthesis enables unprecedented scale in both task count and robot embodiments (over 45 types) without manual collection.

captions.F2: The workflow for data curation and human video generation. As shown in the lower panel, analyzing robot videos, editing frames, generating videos, and evaluating quality are fully automated to synthesize human manipulation videos that share identical semantics under varied visual appearances.

sections.heading: Predicting Videos to Derive Actions: The Zero-WAM Architecture
sections.summary: Zero-WAM is a causal world-action model integrating video generation and action prediction. It takes a human instruction video as a prefix, predicts future robot video chunks, and then outputs executable actions. It also introduces the IFP loss to prevent shortcut learning.
sections.details:
3.1 Preliminaries
Zero-WAM is built upon flow matching for video generation and a causal world-action modeling framework. The joint distribution is factorized into two stages: first predicting future robot video chunks, and then decoding robot action chunks from the predicted video chunks using an inverse dynamics model. It employs a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture, maintaining separate parameters for video and action while enabling interactions via shared attention layers.

3.2 Human Video as Task Specification
When presented with an unseen task at test time, Zero-WAM places the human manipulation video $\mathbf{h}$ at the front of the token sequence as an in-context prompt. The video prediction transformer references this human video context to predict future robot video, whereas the action decoding transformer does not directly attend to the human video; it only references the predicted robot video. This design leverages the fact that once the task intent from the human video is captured in the predicted robot video, action decoding reduces to standard inverse dynamics. To avoid representation mixing between human and robot video latents, a height-wise positional offset is applied in the rotary position embeddings (RoPE).

3.3 In-Context Future Chunk Prediction (IFP)
To prevent the policy from exploiting training shortcuts—predicting immediate actions solely from the robot's own recent history—the authors introduced an auxiliary IFP loss. This objective requires predicting future robot video chunks several steps ahead (with a temporal stride) in parallel from current video representations. The auxiliary prediction module cannot access the human video directly and receives only intermediate representations from the main branch. This forces the main transformer to extract the long-term task progression from the human video and embed it into its representations.

3.4 Training and Inference
Training is conducted on a mixture of Task-diverse VA and HumanGen. At inference time, the IFP module is detached, and the model autonomously generates future video and actions conditioned either on language alone or on human video prompts (ICL mode).

sections.heading: Validation in Simulation and the Real World: Strong Zero-Shot Generalization
sections.summary: Across seven unseen tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator, Zero-WAM achieved a 47.0% success rate, outperforming baselines by 29.5 percentage points. On a real dual-arm robot, it also completed unseen object arrangements and fine insertion tasks guided only by human videos.
sections.details:
4.1 Implementation
Built on the Wan-2.2-TI2V-5B video generation model, Zero-WAM underwent pre-training requiring roughly 15,000 GPU hours. During evaluation in ICL mode, language instructions are omitted, and the model operates purely from human video prompts.

4.2 Simulation Experiments
Among 50 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0, 43 were used for training and 7 were reserved for zero-shot evaluation on unseen tasks (placing an object on a scale, stamping, opening a microwave, moving a stapler, placing bread in a basket, placing a mug, and 3-block stacking).

- WAN-Action (baseline): 10.98% average success rate
- LingBot-VA (strong baseline): 17.45% average success rate
- Zero-WAM (ours): 46.95% average success rate

Zero-WAM outperformed existing methods across all unseen tasks, successfully handling articulated mechanisms like opening a microwave and uniquely achieving successes on 3-block stacking, where all baselines failed completely (0%).

4.3 Real-World Experiments
Evaluations were conducted on a real bimanual Franka robot across three task suites. The model was trained only on a few basic motion trajectories, leaving test configurations entirely unseen except for the provided human video prompt.

- Placing objects into containers: Achieved 53.3% on unseen object and container combinations, exceeding language-guided LingBot-VA (43.3%).
- Three-object sequential manipulation: Reached 33.3% following random sequences specified by human videos, well ahead of LingBot-VA (10.0%).
- Table leg insertion: In a precision task requiring specific colored legs to be inserted into specific holes indicated by video, LingBot-VA scored 0%, while Zero-WAM successfully inserted legs into unseen target holes.

4.4 Ablation Studies
Ablations confirmed the contribution of each design component. Removing IFP caused the unseen task average success rate in simulation to plummet from 46.95% to 28.55%, confirming that shortcut suppression is critical. Additionally, task-balanced sampling during pre-training alone substantially improved performance.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Human Videos as a Bridge Between Robots and the World
sections.summary: This study enables zero-shot adaptation to unseen tasks by using human demonstration videos as prompts. Future work is expected to expand the framework from stationary tabletop setups to mobile manipulation and longer-horizon tasks.
sections.details:
The paper concludes that combining large-scale human video guidance with task-balanced pre-training opens a viable path for robots to execute completely novel tasks on site without any additional training or parameter updates.

The authors outline several avenues for future research:

- Expanding Scope: Experiments in this work focused primarily on stationary tabletop bimanual setups. Extending the framework to mobile manipulation and complex daily activities requiring longer horizons is an important next step.
- Utilizing Egocentric Videos: Unconstrained human daily videos are orders of magnitude more plentiful than robot data. Although an embodiment gap exists, learning task-level semantic correspondence as demonstrated in this work could allow robots to efficiently acquire commonsense knowledge and manipulation skills from vast repositories of human video.

sections.heading: Related Works: Solving Generalization via In-Context Pre-Training Rather than Test-Time Updates
sections.summary: The paper positions Zero-WAM relative to cross-task manipulation, world-action models, and human video transfer in robotics. Zero-WAM stands out by solving unseen tasks purely through prompt conditioning without requiring test-time optimization or manual alignment.
sections.details:
The work situates itself in three main research contexts:

- Cross-Task Manipulation and VLAs: While language-conditioned VLA models are advancing rapidly, the large semantic gap between language and action spaces makes zero-shot cross-task generalization difficult. Some approaches provide robot trajectory demonstrations, but requiring pre-recorded robot trajectories for novel tasks at test time is impractical.
- World-Action Models (WAMs): Predicting future video before decoding actions (e.g., LingBot-VA) is a promising paradigm. Recent works also explore test-time training (TTT) to update internal memory from video at test time. In contrast, Zero-WAM performs pure in-context inference without any test-time optimization or parameter updates.
- Human Videos for Robotics: Prior efforts have learned representations from human videos, but datasets simultaneously offering task diversity, semantic human-robot alignment, and grounding to executable actions have been lacking. Zero-WAM fills this gap with an automated generation pipeline, realizing a practical world-action model that conditions directly on video prompts.

takeaways: Human demonstration videos (visual state evolutions) provide much richer task specifications for unseen robot tasks than language instructions alone.
Paired human-robot data does not need to be collected by hand; synthesizing human videos from robot trajectories using VLMs and generative AI is both practical and effective.
Auxiliary future chunk prediction (IFP) is essential to suppress shortcuts on past robot history and ensure the model genuinely attends to the video prompt.
limitations: Experiments are primarily limited to tabletop manipulation with stationary setups; generalization to mobile manipulation and dynamic open-world environments remains unverified.
The automated human video generation pipeline is computationally expensive and relies on advanced commercial VLMs and proprietary video generation APIs.
For long-horizon, high-precision tasks such as 3-block stacking, while the model moves past 0% success, performance remains in the single digits (9%), indicating challenges in robust execution.
